c.tagline: Where the Rhine and Moselle meet at the historic German Corner

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered and reliable; ranks at the Hauptbahnhof and Altstadt, or order by phone or app

emergency.note: Emergency services are highly reliable; English is often understood by dispatchers in this well-touristed region

hood_desc: Koblenz's picturesque old town, wedged between the Rhine and Moselle rivers and centered on the Deutsches Eck monument where they merge. Cobblestone lanes, half-timbered houses, and riverside promenades make this the tourist heart of the city.

Perched on a plateau across the Rhine, this district is dominated by the massive Ehrenbreitstein Fortress, reachable by cable car with sweeping views over the river valley. Quieter and more residential than the old town below.
A student-friendly neighborhood south of the center around Görresplatz, known for its concentration of bars, pubs, and late-night eateries. The liveliest part of Koblenz after dark.
A calm riverside district along the Moselle, popular for cycling and walking paths with views back toward the fortress. Largely residential with a handful of traditional wine taverns.
The city's modern commercial core, home to the Löhr-Center shopping mall and pedestrianized shopping streets. Less historic charm but the go-to area for retail and everyday errands.

landmarks: Deutsches Eck (German Corner)
At the dramatic confluence of Rhine and Moselle, a colossal equestrian statue of Kaiser Wilhelm I crowns Germany's most symbolic river junction.
Ehrenbreitstein Fortress
One of Europe's mightiest preserved fortresses broods 118 metres above the Rhine, packing museums and unbeatable views within Prussian ramparts.
Koblenz Cable Car (Seilbahn)
Gondolas glide 890 metres across the Rhine from Deutsches Eck to Ehrenbreitstein, offering the definitive aerial photograph of the river confluence.
Basilica of St. Castor
Koblenz's oldest church, a Romanesque basilica consecrated in 836, witnessed the treaty negotiations that divided Charlemagne's empire.
Old Town and Jesuitenplatz
Winding lanes link the Four Towers, baroque squares and the cheeky spitting Schängel fountain, mascot of Koblenz's two-thousand-year history.
Electoral Palace (Kurfürstliches Schloss)
A refined neoclassical palace of the last Trier prince-elector fronts the Rhine with rose gardens and a grand riverside promenade.
Stolzenfels Castle
Prussian king Frederick William IV's dreamy neo-Gothic summer castle, a UNESCO Rhine Gorge jewel, rises golden above the river south of town.
Church of Our Lady (Liebfrauenkirche)
Its twin baroque onion towers crown the old town's highest point, blending Romanesque, Gothic and baroque across eight centuries.
Rhine Promenade (Konrad-Adenauer-Ufer)
A flower-lined riverside walk sweeps from the Electoral Palace to Deutsches Eck, with castle-crowned vistas and passing river cruisers.
Marksburg Castle
A short trip downstream stands the only Rhine hill castle never destroyed, its 700-year-old halls, kitchens and armory wonderfully intact.

train.note: Koblenz Hauptbahnhof sits about 1.5 km south-west of the Deutsches Eck, an easy 20-minute walk or a short bus ride into the old town. It is the junction of both Rhine main lines and the Moselle line, so ICE and IC trains reach Cologne in about an hour and Frankfurt in 1h30, and a direct regional service runs up the Moselle valley through Trier to Luxembourg City in roughly 2h30 - scenic, cheap and covered by regional fares as far as the border. OeBB Nightjet sleepers between Amsterdam and Switzerland pass through overnight and can be boarded here, though at awkward hours. The left-bank line through Koblenz is also the classic slow way to see the UNESCO Middle Rhine gorge from a train window.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the stops beside Koblenz Hauptbahnhof rather than a dedicated terminal. FlixBus is effectively the only operator here and tickets are bought online. Cologne is about 1h30 by coach and Frankfurt around 2h; for most international journeys you change in Cologne or Frankfurt, both of which have far denser European coach networks.

intl.to: Boppard, St Goar & Rudesheim (Germany) - Middle Rhine sailings from the Rhine promenade landing stages near the Deutsches Eck

ferry.note: Koblenz is 300 km from the sea so there are no sea ferries, but it is the northern gateway to the UNESCO Middle Rhine and one of the best places in Germany to actually travel by scheduled river boat. KD sails upstream past the Lorelei to Boppard, St Goar and Rudesheim from the promenade landings near the Deutsches Eck, mainly April to October and thinning out at the ends of the season. Small local ferries also cross the Rhine and the Moselle within the city all year and carry bicycles. Most people sail one way and return by train on the parallel Rhine line.

half.name: Boppard
half.blurb: A Roman fort site and a wide bend in the Rhine framed by vineyard-covered hillsides mark this river town.

half.name: Cochem
half.blurb: A reconstructed hilltop castle, Reichsburg Cochem, overlooks a wine town on a horseshoe bend of the Moselle River.

half.name: Burg Eltz
half.blurb: A turreted medieval castle, owned by the same family for over 800 years, sits on a rock spur above a Moselle tributary.

half.name: Trier
half.blurb: Germany's oldest city holds the Porta Nigra, a black-sandstone Roman gate, along with Roman baths and an amphitheater.
